moments.title: Arkwright's Cromford Mill
moments.body: Arkwright opens a water-powered cotton-spinning mill at Cromford, Derbyshire. He brings together unrelated workers under a single roof, sets shift hours by clock, and pays wages. This is the prototype of the factory system. Within decades cotton mills dominate Lancashire and Derbyshire.
moments.takeaway: The factory isn't just a building — it's a way of organising labour. Time discipline, supervision, and the wage relationship replace household production.

moments.title: The factory exposes its costs
moments.body: Friedrich Engels's 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' (1845) documents Manchester's slums. Child labour, 12-14 hour days, industrial disease. The Factory Acts (1833 onwards) begin restricting working hours for children — early industrial regulation.

quote.text: Manchester... contains 400,000 inhabitants, rather more than less... the cottages are old, dirty, and of the smallest sort, the streets uneven, fallen into ruts and in part without drains or pavement.
quote.attrib: Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England

moments.takeaway: The industrial business model created enormous productivity gains and equally enormous social costs. The regulatory response was political, not automatic.

now.title: After the factory
now.body: The 20th century added the assembly line (Ford, 1913), scientific management (Taylor), then the post-Fordist service economy. The factory model survives — Foxconn, Amazon warehouses, Vietnamese garment factories — but is increasingly outsourced. The 'gig economy' returns to forms of piecework that pre-date the factory.
now.open_questions: Is platform work (Uber, Deliveroo) a return to pre-industrial piecework or something new? It has elements of both — algorithmic supervision combined with the absence of employment status.

items.reflection: The factory system is the foundation everything else in business studies sits on. Without 1771-1830, no modern firm, no modern management theory, no modern industrial relations.

moments.title: Principles of Scientific Management
moments.body: Taylor publishes his methods of breaking tasks into measurable components, timing each motion with a stopwatch, and prescribing the 'one best way'. His earlier work at Bethlehem Steel had shown massive productivity gains — and equally massive worker hostility.

quote.text: In the past the man has been first; in the future the system must be first.
quote.attrib: F.W. Taylor, Principles of Scientific Management

moments.takeaway: Taylorism treats workers as physical components of a production system. It maximises throughput; it strips out worker autonomy.

moments.title: The Hawthorne Studies
moments.who: Elton Mayo and team, Western Electric's Hawthorne Works, Chicago
moments.body: Originally designed to test how lighting affected productivity, the studies found productivity rose under almost any change — including reduced lighting. The interpretation: workers responded to being observed and consulted ('Hawthorne effect'). Subsequent interviews emphasised social and emotional factors.
moments.takeaway: Hawthorne is the founding moment of the 'human relations' school. Productivity is not just engineering — it's psychology and group dynamics. Later re-analysis suggests the original data is messier than the textbook story implies, but the interpretation reshaped management thought.

now.title: After Taylor and Mayo
now.body: Management theory now incorporates both — process engineering (Six Sigma, Lean) and human factors (engagement, culture, well-being). The 21st-century knowledge economy further complicates things: how do you 'time and motion' a software engineer? Algorithmic management at platforms like Amazon and Uber arguably reintroduces Taylorism with sensors and dashboards instead of stopwatches.
now.open_questions: Can scientific management coexist with worker autonomy and creativity? The lean/agile/sociotechnical traditions try; the question of whether they succeed is still open.

items.reflection: Taylor's stopwatch and Mayo's interview are the two methodological poles of management. Every contemporary HR or operations practice descends from one, the other, or the attempt to balance them.

moments.title: Model T launched
moments.who: Henry Ford and the Ford Motor Company
moments.body: Ford introduces the Model T in October 1908 at $850 — already cheaper than competitors. He aims to make 'a car for the great multitude'.
moments.takeaway: Ford had been making cars since 1903. The Model T was the design that made mass-market motoring imaginable.

moments.title: The moving assembly line
moments.who: Ford engineers at Highland Park, Michigan
moments.body: The moving assembly line is introduced. Magneto assembly time falls from 20 minutes to 5. By 1914 the entire chassis can be built in 93 minutes (down from 12.5 hours). The Model T's price falls below $300 by the mid-1920s. Production peaks at over 2 million per year.

quote.text: Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants so long as it is black.
quote.attrib: Henry Ford, My Life and Work, 1922

moments.takeaway: The assembly line trades flexibility for radical cost reduction. Standardisation creates a consumer good that can be afforded by the workers who make it.

moments.title: Model T discontinued
moments.body: GM under Alfred Sloan introduces annual model changes, multiple price points and consumer credit. Ford's single-model strategy is overtaken. The Model T is discontinued; the Model A is launched in 1927. Ford loses market leadership.
moments.takeaway: The first-mover advantage in mass production doesn't last forever. Sloan's segmentation strategy at GM defines automotive marketing for the rest of the century.

now.title: After Fordism
now.body: Toyota's lean production (1950s-1970s) replaced Fordist mass production with flexible specialisation: just-in-time inventory, kaizen continuous improvement, worker problem-solving authority. The 1990 MIT IMVP study ('The Machine That Changed the World') made lean the dominant manufacturing paradigm. Modern car plants — and Amazon warehouses, hospitals, software teams — apply variants of lean thinking.
now.open_questions: Has Toyota's just-in-time model become a vulnerability? The COVID-19 supply chain disruptions of 2020-22 forced a reconsideration of buffer inventory and 'just-in-case' thinking.

items.reflection: Ford taught the world to mass-produce. Toyota taught it to mass-customise. Most subsequent operations management is a refinement of one or the other.

moments.title: Toyota Motor Co. founded
moments.body: Toyota begins as a spin-off from Toyoda Automatic Loom Works. The family name had used a 't' (Toyoda) — the new company chose 'Toyota' for fewer brushstrokes and clearer pronunciation.
moments.takeaway: Toyota's later innovations grew from a textile company's deep familiarity with autonomous machinery (jidoka — machines that stop when something goes wrong).

moments.title: Taiichi Ohno develops the Toyota Production System
moments.body: After WWII, Toyota cannot afford Detroit-style mass production. Ohno develops a system designed around small batches, fast changeovers, defect elimination, and worker problem-solving. Just-in-time inventory, kanban cards, andon cords (workers can stop the line) all emerge. The model is partly inspired by US supermarkets — replenishing shelves only when items are taken.

quote.text: Costs do not exist to be calculated. Costs exist to be reduced.

moments.takeaway: TPS turns Fordism inside out: instead of large buffers absorbing problems, problems must be visible and fixed immediately.

moments.title: The Machine That Changed the World
moments.who: James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos, MIT International Motor Vehicle Program
moments.body: The MIT study compares automotive plants worldwide and finds Japanese 'lean' producers dramatically outperform Western mass producers on productivity, quality and inventory. The book popularises 'lean production' as a term and makes Toyota the global benchmark.
moments.takeaway: Lean spreads beyond automotive — into electronics, healthcare, software (lean startup, agile).

now.title: Lean as orthodoxy and its critics
now.body: Lean is now standard taught content in operations management. Variants include Lean Six Sigma, lean startup (Eric Ries, 2011), lean healthcare. Critics note that lean intensifies work (less buffer = more pressure) and that JIT supply chains are fragile to shocks (Fukushima 2011, semiconductor shortages, COVID).
now.open_questions: Can lean coexist with resilience? Toyota itself emphasises long-term supplier relationships and risk management — but the 'lean' label has often been applied more aggressively elsewhere.

items.reflection: A post-war Japanese carmaker, working under cash constraints, invented a system that became the global standard. Constraint isn't only a problem — sometimes it's the source of better ideas.

moments.title: The Wealth of Nations
moments.body: Smith publishes 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' on 9 March 1776. The opening chapters describe a pin factory: one worker alone can produce a handful of pins per day; ten workers, each specialised, produce 48,000 between them.

quote.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
quote.attrib: Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter II

moments.takeaway: Specialisation and exchange — not just hard work — explain the wealth gap between societies. The pin factory becomes the canonical example of division of labour in business teaching.

now.title: Smith in modern business
now.body: Smith's specialisation principle underlies every modern firm structure and supply chain. Globalised production extends division of labour across countries. Smith himself warned about the cognitive costs of extreme specialisation ('The man whose whole life is spent in performing a few simple operations... generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become').
now.open_questions: Where are the limits of specialisation in knowledge work, where general judgment matters more than narrow expertise?

items.reflection: Smith is invoked for free markets and forgotten for his warnings. The actual text is more cautious than its reputation.

moments.title: East India Company chartered
moments.body: On 31 December 1600, the Honourable East India Company receives its royal charter. It is a joint-stock company: shares are sold to investors, who share profits in proportion to their stake. It was not the first joint-stock venture, but it became the largest and longest-lived.
moments.takeaway: Pooling capital from many small investors makes ventures possible that no individual could finance.

moments.title: Limited liability becomes general
moments.body: The Limited Liability Act 1855 and the Joint Stock Companies Act 1856, consolidated in 1862, generalise limited liability incorporation for the first time. Shareholders' losses are capped at their investment; personal assets are protected.
moments.takeaway: The combination of joint-stock ownership and limited liability is the legal foundation of the modern public company.

now.title: Companies today
now.body: By 2024 the UK had over 5 million registered companies (Companies House). The corporate form has been extended (B Corps, public benefit corporations, employee ownership trusts) but the joint-stock limited company remains the dominant structure for serious commercial activity.
now.open_questions: Should limited liability extend to all corporate harm? Recent debates on environmental and human rights liability test the limits.

items.reflection: Limited liability was controversial in 1855 — critics argued it would encourage reckless speculation. The corporate form we treat as natural is a 19th-century legal innovation.

moments.title: The Practice of Management
moments.body: Drucker publishes 'The Practice of Management', arguing that management is a distinct professional discipline and that the firm's purpose is to create a customer. He introduces 'management by objectives' as a framework.

quote.text: There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer.

moments.takeaway: Management before Drucker was a craft passed on within firms. After, it became a teachable discipline with its own literature.

moments.title: Knowledge worker named
moments.body: Drucker coins 'knowledge worker' to describe the post-industrial labour force. The implication: productivity in knowledge work needs different tools from physical work.
moments.takeaway: By the 2020s, knowledge work makes up the majority of employment in advanced economies — a transition Drucker named decades early.

now.title: Drucker's legacy
now.body: Drucker's MBO is now taught alongside more recent variants (OKRs, used at Intel from Andy Grove in the 1970s and at Google from 1999). The shift from manufacturing to knowledge work continues to drive changes in how firms are managed.
now.open_questions: How do you measure productivity in knowledge work? It's still an unresolved problem, sharpened by remote work post-2020.

items.reflection: Drucker wrote 39 books across 65 years. The breadth — economics, sociology, ethics, management practice — is hard to imitate now that academic disciplines are more siloed.

moments.title: How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy
moments.body: Porter's Harvard Business Review article introduces the five forces framework: rivalry, buyer power, supplier power, threat of entry, threat of substitutes. The article is one of HBR's most-reprinted.
moments.takeaway: Strategy is reframed from competitor-by-competitor analysis to industry-structure analysis.

moments.title: Competitive Strategy
moments.body: Porter's book extends the five forces framework and introduces three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, focus. The book becomes the most-cited strategy text of the 1980s and 1990s.
moments.takeaway: Strategy becomes a discipline with explicit frameworks, taught in MBA programmes worldwide.

moments.title: Competitive Advantage
moments.body: The follow-up introduces the value chain — disaggregating a firm into primary and support activities to identify where competitive advantage can be built.
moments.takeaway: Internal analysis joins external analysis in Porter's framework.

now.title: Porter today
now.body: Five forces is still the most-taught industry framework in business education. Critics (W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne's 'Blue Ocean Strategy', 2005) argue Porter underweights innovation in creating new markets rather than competing in existing ones. Platform economics and network effects complicate the original framework.
now.open_questions: How do five forces apply to multi-sided platforms (Uber, Airbnb) where the 'buyer' and 'supplier' distinction is fuzzy?

items.reflection: Porter's frameworks were criticised in the 2000s as too static; they have outlived most of the critiques.

moments.title: Reengineering Work: Don't Automate, Obliterate
moments.body: Hammer's HBR article argues that IT investments fail when they automate existing processes rather than redesigning them. The piece becomes a starting gun for the business process reengineering movement.
moments.takeaway: Technology applied to broken processes produces faster broken processes.

moments.title: Reengineering the Corporation
moments.body: The book sells over 2 million copies. Firms launch radical process redesigns, often associated with mass layoffs.
moments.takeaway: BPR becomes both a strategic management tool and a euphemism for redundancy programmes.

now.title: BPR after the hype
now.body: By the late 1990s, surveys found 50-70% of BPR programmes failed to deliver expected benefits. Champy himself wrote a follow-up acknowledging that the human side had been underweighted. BPR ideas survive in digital transformation, RPA (robotic process automation) and 'process mining' analytics. Hammer died in 2008.
now.open_questions: How much organisational disruption can a firm absorb before performance falls? BPR underestimated the answer.

items.reflection: Management fashions follow predictable arcs: bold claim, mass adoption, disappointing average results, quiet absorption into mainstream practice.

moments.title: Netscape IPO
moments.body: Netscape goes public on 9 August 1995. Priced at $28, it opens at $71 and closes at $58 — a 16-month-old company with no profits valued at $2.7bn on day one. The IPO is widely credited with launching the dot-com boom.
moments.takeaway: Public markets begin pricing internet companies on traffic and 'eyeballs' rather than profits.

moments.title: Nasdaq peak and crash
moments.body: The Nasdaq Composite peaks at 5,048 on 10 March 2000. By October 2002 it has fallen to 1,114 — a 78% drop. Pets.com (founded 1998, IPO February 2000, liquidated November 2000) becomes the symbol of the era.
moments.takeaway: Most dot-com casualties were over-capitalised on flawed business models. A minority (Amazon, eBay, Google) survived to dominate.

now.title: After the crash
now.body: The surviving firms reshape the economy. Amazon, founded 1994, is now valued over $1.5tn. The 2020-21 tech boom and 2022 correction repeated patterns from 2000 (high valuations, falling earnings ratios, post-correction shake-out) at larger scale.
now.open_questions: Are AI-era valuations a bubble, durable, or both? The post-2022 pattern is unresolved.

items.reflection: Bubbles are usually built on real innovations. The trouble is that the innovation's value rarely accrues to the firms first marketed as its beneficiaries.

moments.title: Cracks appear
moments.who: Subprime lenders, BNP Paribas, Northern Rock
moments.body: US subprime mortgage delinquencies rise sharply through 2007. BNP Paribas freezes three funds in August 2007 citing inability to value mortgage-backed assets. Northern Rock requests Bank of England emergency liquidity in September, triggering the first UK bank run since 1866.
moments.takeaway: Wholesale funding markets seize first; retail customers see the consequences later.

moments.title: Lehman Brothers files Chapter 11
moments.who: Lehman Brothers, US Treasury, Bank of England
moments.body: On 15 September 2008, Lehman Brothers files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy — the largest in US history at $639bn in assets. The Treasury and Federal Reserve declined to support a rescue, in contrast with the Bear Stearns intervention earlier that year. Credit markets freeze worldwide.
moments.takeaway: A single failure transmitted through global counterparty exposures within hours.

moments.title: Rescue, recession, regulation
moments.body: Massive coordinated rescues follow: TARP ($700bn) in the US, RBS and Lloyds part-nationalised in the UK, quantitative easing programmes globally. The Dodd-Frank Act (2010) and Basel III (2010-13) overhaul financial regulation.
moments.takeaway: Crisis triggered the largest peacetime increase in financial regulation since the 1930s.

now.title: After 2008
now.body: Regulators imposed higher capital, liquidity and resolution requirements. Stress tests became routine. The 2023 collapses of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse showed the new framework constrained but did not eliminate banking crises. Risk migrated to less-regulated 'shadow banking' (private credit, non-bank intermediation).
now.open_questions: Has the financial system been made resilient, or has risk been pushed to less-visible corners?

items.reflection: The 2008 crisis exposed not just bad lending but failures of risk modelling, rating agencies and regulatory frameworks. Its consequences still shape monetary and fiscal policy a generation later.

moments.title: UberCab launches in San Francisco
moments.body: Uber (initially UberCab) launches in San Francisco. The model: matching riders and drivers through a smartphone app, with the platform setting prices and rating drivers. Drivers are classified as independent contractors, not employees.
moments.takeaway: Smartphone GPS plus payment infrastructure enabled a labour-market structure that wasn't operationally feasible before 2007.

moments.title: Platform proliferation
moments.body: Platform firms extend across sectors: short-term rentals, food delivery, freelance work. By 2019 ONS estimated 4.7% of UK workers had done gig economy work in the past year. US estimates ranged from 5-36% depending on definition.
moments.takeaway: Platform work blurred the line between employment and entrepreneurship across a wide range of activities.

moments.title: Uber drivers ruled workers in UK
moments.who: UK Supreme Court, Aslam v Uber BV
moments.body: The Supreme Court rules unanimously on 19 February 2021 that Uber drivers are 'workers' for the purposes of UK employment law — entitled to minimum wage and paid leave but not full employee rights.
moments.takeaway: Courts in multiple jurisdictions are reshaping the employment status of platform workers.

now.title: Gig work today
now.body: EU Platform Work Directive (provisionally agreed 2024) creates a presumption of employment for platform workers meeting certain criteria. California's Prop 22 (2020) went the other way, exempting Uber and Lyft drivers from employee status. Litigation continues globally.
now.open_questions: Will platform work converge on a new intermediate status, or be pushed back toward employment? Regulators in different jurisdictions are making different choices.

items.reflection: The gig economy revived a debate older than the Factory Acts about who counts as an employee and what protections employment brings. The 19th-century categories are under pressure but have not yet been replaced.

moments.title: Owen takes over New Lanark
moments.body: Owen runs New Lanark cotton mills with shorter hours, infant schools and worker housing while remaining profitable.
moments.takeaway: Profit and welfare can coexist with deliberate management design.

moments.title: New Harmony, Indiana
moments.body: Owen's utopian community fails within three years but inspires the cooperative movement.
moments.takeaway: Utopian experiments often inform later reforms even when they fail.

moments.title: Rochdale Pioneers
moments.body: Rochdale codifies cooperative principles that spread globally to retail, banking and platforms.
moments.takeaway: Owen's legacy lives in the cooperative movement.

now.title: Social enterprise today
now.body: B-Corps, social enterprises and ESG frameworks revive the Owenite combination of welfare and profit.
now.open_questions: Can social enterprise scale to dominant sectors of the economy?

items.reflection: Owen's mix of philanthropy, business and utopianism prefigures contemporary social enterprise.

moments.title: Limited Liability Act
moments.body: The Act allows shareholders' liability to be limited to their investment, after decades of debate.
moments.takeaway: Limited liability had to be argued for, not assumed.

moments.title: Companies Act consolidated
moments.body: The 1862 Act consolidates company law, making the limited liability company the standard British business form.
moments.takeaway: Standard incorporation reshaped capital allocation.

moments.title: Joint Stock Companies Act precedent
moments.body: The 1856 Act made incorporation by simple registration possible, building on the 1844 Act.
moments.takeaway: Incremental statutory change underpinned the modern corporation.

now.title: The corporation today
now.body: Limited liability remains the foundation of corporate capitalism; debates focus on stakeholder accountability and corporate governance.
now.open_questions: Should limited liability be conditional on social and environmental performance?

items.reflection: The modern corporation is a statutory creation, not a natural form.

moments.title: Illumination studies begin
moments.body: Western Electric's lighting studies produce confusing results: productivity rises whether illumination goes up or down.
moments.takeaway: Confounds in field studies can yield more interesting findings than intended.

moments.title: Relay assembly studies conclude
moments.body: Long-term observation of a small assembly group identifies social factors and supervisory style as productivity drivers.
moments.takeaway: Workers respond to attention, not just incentives.

moments.title: The Social Problems of an Industrial Civilization
moments.body: Mayo's book frames the human relations school's response to scientific management.
moments.takeaway: Management theory branches into social-psychological terrain.

now.title: Human relations today
now.body: Engagement, culture and psychological safety draw on the human relations lineage; algorithmic management partly reverses the trend.
now.open_questions: Can human relations principles be implemented through software?

items.reflection: Hawthorne is taught everywhere; its data is messier than the textbook story.

moments.title: A Theory of Human Motivation
moments.body: Maslow's Psychological Review paper proposes a hierarchy from physiological needs to self-actualisation.
moments.takeaway: Motivation can be ordered hierarchically.

moments.title: Motivation and Personality
moments.body: Maslow's book extends the hierarchy and feeds into the human potential movement.
moments.takeaway: Humanistic psychology fed into management theory.

moments.title: Hierarchy critiques
moments.body: Empirical tests fail to validate strict hierarchy; cross-cultural studies challenge Maslow's universality claims.
moments.takeaway: Iconic pyramids do not always survive testing.

now.title: Beyond Maslow
now.body: Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) and job characteristics model (Hackman and Oldham) replace Maslow in research, while the pyramid persists in textbooks.
now.open_questions: Why does the Maslow pyramid persist in teaching despite weak empirical support?

items.reflection: Maslow himself never drew the pyramid; later teachers added it.

moments.title: The Motivation to Work
moments.body: Herzberg's interviews with Pittsburgh engineers and accountants distinguish hygiene factors (which prevent dissatisfaction) from motivators (which cause satisfaction).
moments.takeaway: Job satisfaction and dissatisfaction may have different causes.

moments.title: One More Time: How Do You Motivate Employees?
moments.body: Herzberg's Harvard Business Review article becomes one of HBR's most reprinted, popularising 'KITA' management.
moments.takeaway: HBR articles can outlast academic books in shaping practice.

moments.title: Job characteristics model
moments.body: Hackman and Oldham develop a more empirically robust model of intrinsic motivation through skill variety, task identity, autonomy and feedback.
moments.takeaway: Successor models replaced Herzberg in research.

now.title: Motivation in modern work
now.body: Job design, autonomy, and intrinsic motivation continue to draw on the Herzberg lineage. Remote and gig work challenge the framework.
now.open_questions: How do gig workers' hygiene and motivator factors differ from traditional employees?

items.reflection: Herzberg's two-factor model is widely taught and contested in equal measure.

moments.title: The Human Side of Enterprise lecture
moments.body: McGregor introduces Theory X (workers need control) and Theory Y (workers seek responsibility) as assumptions managers hold.
moments.takeaway: Managerial assumptions become self-fulfilling.

moments.title: The Human Side of Enterprise book
moments.body: McGregor's book consolidates Theory X/Y and frames management as a choice between assumptions.
moments.takeaway: A simple binary can reshape management training.

moments.title: Theory Z
moments.body: Ouchi extends the framework with Theory Z, drawing on Japanese management practice.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural comparison reshaped Western management.

now.title: Beyond X and Y
now.body: Modern management theory uses transformational and servant leadership models; X/Y remains a teaching staple.
now.open_questions: Are algorithmic management systems implicitly Theory X?

items.reflection: McGregor's binary persists because it is teachable, not because it is empirically robust.

moments.title: Ohno joins Toyota machine shop
moments.body: Ohno begins the long development of what becomes the Toyota Production System.
moments.takeaway: TPS evolved over decades, not in a single insight.

moments.title: Toyota Production System book
moments.body: Ohno's book finally documents TPS for an external audience, emphasising waste elimination and continuous improvement.
moments.takeaway: Tacit operations knowledge took decades to externalise.

moments.title: The Machine That Changed the World
moments.body: Womack, Jones and Roos's book popularises 'lean production' for a global management audience.
moments.takeaway: Industry studies can re-export production methods.

now.title: Lean beyond manufacturing
now.body: Lean startup (Eric Ries 2011), lean software, lean healthcare and lean services all extend TPS principles.
now.open_questions: Has just-in-time become a vulnerability under climate and geopolitical shocks?

items.reflection: Ohno worked in obscurity for decades before TPS became management theory's reference point.

moments.title: Concept of the Corporation
moments.body: Drucker's study of General Motors helps invent management consulting and modern management writing.
moments.takeaway: Empirical study of a single firm could ground a discipline.

moments.title: The Practice of Management
moments.body: Drucker introduces management by objectives (MBO) as a self-directed performance system.
moments.takeaway: Management could be taught as a discipline.

moments.title: The Age of Discontinuity
moments.body: Drucker coins 'knowledge worker' and 'knowledge economy', anticipating the post-industrial shift.
moments.takeaway: Drucker's vocabulary outlasted many of his prescriptions.

now.title: Drucker's continuing influence
now.body: Drucker's vocabulary still saturates management writing. The Drucker Institute continues to develop his frameworks.
now.open_questions: How does AI alter Drucker's knowledge worker concept?

items.reflection: Drucker wrote 39 books over 60 years and shaped management as a recognised profession.

moments.title: Strategies for Diversification
moments.body: Ansoff's HBR article introduces the four-quadrant matrix of market penetration, market development, product development and diversification.
moments.takeaway: Strategic options could be classified systematically.

moments.title: Corporate Strategy
moments.body: Ansoff's book systematises strategic planning, distinguishing strategic, administrative and operating decisions.
moments.takeaway: Strategic management became a teachable discipline.

moments.title: Strategic Management journal founded
moments.body: The new journal institutionalises the field that Ansoff and contemporaries had defined.
moments.takeaway: Institutionalisation follows founding texts.

now.title: Ansoff matrix today
now.body: The Ansoff matrix remains a standard tool in business education, alongside more dynamic strategy frameworks.
now.open_questions: Does the Ansoff matrix capture platform-style strategy?

items.reflection: Ansoff combined Soviet-emigre mathematics training with American corporate experience.

moments.title: Business Policy: Text and Cases
moments.body: The Harvard textbook formalises SWOT-style analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
moments.takeaway: SWOT emerged from Harvard Business School case method.

moments.title: The Concept of Corporate Strategy
moments.body: Andrews defines strategy as the matching of internal capabilities and external opportunities.
moments.takeaway: Strategy as a fit became an enduring framing.

moments.title: SWOT spreads
moments.body: Weihrich's TOWS matrix formalises SWOT and spreads it through consulting practice.
moments.takeaway: Consulting carries academic frameworks into business.

now.title: SWOT today
now.body: SWOT is ubiquitous in business education and consulting despite frequent criticism of its lack of rigour.
now.open_questions: Does SWOT analysis encourage strategic thinking or merely list items?

items.reflection: SWOT's persistence reflects how strategic frameworks must above all be teachable.

moments.title: Competitive Advantage
moments.body: Porter introduces the value chain as a framework for analysing how firms create value through linked activities.
moments.takeaway: Strategy descends to operations through the value chain.

moments.title: The Competitive Advantage of Nations
moments.body: Porter extends competitive analysis to national economies with the diamond model.
moments.takeaway: Competitive advantage scales from firm to nation.

moments.title: What Is Strategy?
moments.body: Porter argues strategy is about doing different things or doing the same things differently, distinguishing it from operational effectiveness.
moments.takeaway: Strategic positioning is more than benchmarking.

now.title: Value chain in global supply chains
now.body: Global value chain research extends Porter's framework to international production networks.
now.open_questions: How does the value chain framework adapt to platform business models?

items.reflection: Porter's frameworks dominate business school strategy teaching despite increasing critique.

moments.title: Basic Marketing
moments.body: McCarthy's textbook crystallises the 4 Ps (Product, Price, Place, Promotion) as a marketing teaching framework.
moments.takeaway: Mnemonics shape teaching.

moments.title: Marketing Management
moments.body: Kotler's textbook codifies marketing as a discipline; it remains in print across multiple editions.
moments.takeaway: Textbooks consolidate disciplines.

moments.title: 7 Ps for services
moments.body: Booms and Bitner add People, Process and Physical evidence for services marketing.
moments.takeaway: Service marketing required framework extension.

now.title: Marketing in digital era
now.body: Digital marketing, performance marketing and growth hacking sit alongside the classical 4 Ps in modern teaching.
now.open_questions: Do the 4 Ps still organise marketing in algorithmically mediated commerce?

items.reflection: McCarthy's 4 Ps have persisted for 65 years as a teaching device, despite recurring proposals to replace them.

moments.title: Deming lectures in Japan
moments.body: Deming's lectures on statistical quality control help shape postwar Japanese manufacturing.
moments.takeaway: Statistical methods underpinned Japan's quality revolution.

moments.title: Out of the Crisis
moments.body: Deming's book sets out his 14 points for management, contrasting Japanese and US practice.
moments.takeaway: Quality is built in by management, not inspected in.

moments.title: Six Sigma at Motorola
moments.body: Motorola develops Six Sigma to achieve 3.4 defects per million opportunities, building on Deming's statistical foundations.
moments.takeaway: Quality methods institutionalised as named programs.

now.title: Quality in modern operations
now.body: Lean Six Sigma combines TPS waste-elimination and Six Sigma variation-reduction in healthcare, services and software.
now.open_questions: How do agile and lean traditions interact in modern software operations?

items.reflection: Deming was unknown in the US for decades while shaping Japanese industry.

moments.title: Don't Automate, Obliterate
moments.body: Hammer's HBR article calls for radical redesign of business processes rather than incremental automation.
moments.takeaway: A provocative framing launched a management wave.

moments.title: Reengineering the Corporation
moments.body: Their book popularises business process reengineering; many initial implementations involve major layoffs.
moments.takeaway: Reengineering became synonymous with downsizing in practice.

moments.title: Reengineering Revolution backlash
moments.body: Hammer publicly acknowledges that BPR projects too often degenerated into cost-cutting exercises.
moments.takeaway: Management fashions often disappoint their authors.

now.title: Process management today
now.body: Business process management, RPA and AI workflow tools carry forward reengineering's analytical ambitions in lighter form.
now.open_questions: Will AI deliver on reengineering's original promise of radical productivity change?

items.reflection: BPR was the dominant management fashion of the early 1990s and a cautionary tale by the late 1990s.

moments.title: Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach
moments.body: Freeman's book argues firms should be managed for stakeholders, not only shareholders.
moments.takeaway: Stakeholder theory entered strategic management.

moments.title: Stakeholder Capitalism
moments.body: Business Roundtable and EU debates push stakeholder capitalism into corporate governance.
moments.takeaway: Public discourse periodically reopens the stakeholder question.

moments.title: Business Roundtable redefines corporate purpose
moments.body: 181 CEOs sign a statement committing to all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
moments.takeaway: Even the home of shareholder primacy formally adopted stakeholder language.

now.title: Stakeholder governance in practice
now.body: ESG investing, B-Corps and SDG-linked reporting operationalise stakeholder principles, though critics question implementation.
now.open_questions: Does stakeholder governance change behaviour or only rhetoric?

items.reflection: Freeman's theoretical move took 35 years to reach mainstream corporate language.

moments.title: Three-Dimensional CSR Model
moments.body: Carroll's framework distinguishes economic, legal, ethical and discretionary responsibilities of business.
moments.takeaway: CSR could be analysed as layered responsibilities.

moments.title: Pyramid of CSR
moments.body: Carroll arranges the four CSR domains into a pyramid model that becomes a standard teaching framework.
moments.takeaway: A visual model spread CSR rapidly into business education.

moments.title: Triple Bottom Line
moments.body: Elkington coins 'triple bottom line' (people, planet, profit), framing sustainable business reporting.
moments.takeaway: Sustainability acquired its own accounting language.

now.title: CSR to ESG
now.body: ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) frameworks have largely displaced CSR in financial markets and corporate reporting.
now.open_questions: Does ESG integration change corporate behaviour or only disclosure?

items.reflection: Carroll's pyramid is taught everywhere; Elkington has since 'recalled' the triple bottom line as inadequate.

moments.title: Disruptive technologies
moments.body: Their HBR article argues incumbents fail not from incompetence but from listening too closely to existing customers.
moments.takeaway: Success can produce predictable failure.

moments.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
moments.body: Christensen's book uses disk drive and other industries to illustrate disruptive innovation.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical framework gained massive cross-industry uptake.

moments.title: What Is Disruptive Innovation?
moments.body: Christensen reclaims the term from misuse, restricting it to specific market entry patterns.
moments.takeaway: Theorists struggle to control how their concepts spread.

now.title: Disruption today
now.body: Disruption is now invoked in nearly every industry, often loosely. Christensen's actual framework requires specific conditions.
now.open_questions: Is generative AI a Christensen-style disruption or a different pattern?

items.reflection: Few academic books have shaped business vocabulary as much as Christensen's.

moments.title: Culture's Consequences
moments.body: Hofstede's analysis of IBM employee surveys in 40 countries identifies four cultural dimensions.
moments.takeaway: Within-firm surveys generated a foundational cross-cultural dataset.

moments.title: Cultures and Organizations
moments.body: Hofstede adds long-term orientation as a fifth dimension drawing on Chinese Value Survey.
moments.takeaway: Dimensions are extended as evidence accumulates.

moments.title: Indulgence vs Restraint added
moments.body: A sixth dimension is added in the updated edition of Cultures and Organizations.
moments.takeaway: Models evolve over decades.

now.title: Cross-cultural management today
now.body: Hofstede's dimensions remain heavily used despite GLOBE study competition and methodological critiques.
now.open_questions: Are cultural dimensions stable enough to support 2020s business decisions?

items.reflection: Hofstede's dataset gave cross-cultural management a quantitative spine, for better and worse.

moments.title: Welch becomes GE CEO
moments.body: Welch takes over GE and pursues 'be number 1 or 2' in each market, divesting or fixing the rest.
moments.takeaway: Strategy became aggressive portfolio management.

moments.title: Pick and Choose speech
moments.body: Welch's New York speech often dated as the start of the shareholder value era.
moments.takeaway: A speech can mark a strategic era.

moments.title: Welch retires
moments.body: Welch retires with GE valued at over $400bn. Successor Jeffrey Immelt inherits an increasingly financial firm.
moments.takeaway: Strategic eras often end with succession problems.

now.title: After Welch
now.body: GE's spinout into three separate companies in 2021-24 closes the Welch era. Stakeholder, ESG and long-termism debates partly respond to his legacy.
now.open_questions: How will the Welch playbook be evaluated by business historians in 50 years?

items.reflection: Welch was Fortune's manager of the century in 1999; his model is now widely criticised.

moments.title: Jobs returns to Apple
moments.body: Apple is weeks from bankruptcy; Jobs returns as interim CEO and cuts the product line drastically.
moments.takeaway: Strategic focus rescued a near-bankrupt firm.

moments.title: iPod launched
moments.body: The iPod launches in October 2001, beginning Apple's integrated hardware-software-content strategy.
moments.takeaway: Integrated product strategy reshaped consumer electronics.

moments.title: iPhone launched
moments.body: The iPhone launches in January 2007, redefining the smartphone category.
moments.takeaway: Single product launches can redefine industries.

now.title: Apple after Jobs
now.body: Under Tim Cook, Apple becomes the world's most valuable company, expanding services revenue and supply chain mastery.
now.open_questions: Can Apple sustain its margins as smartphone growth plateaus?

items.reflection: Jobs's death in 2011 closed an era; Apple's continued dominance has surprised many who expected drift without him.

moments.title: Enron's peak
moments.body: Enron is named Fortune's most innovative company for six consecutive years through 2001.
moments.takeaway: Awards lag fundamentals.

moments.title: Enron bankruptcy
moments.body: Enron files for bankruptcy in December 2001 after accounting fraud is exposed. Arthur Andersen, the auditor, collapses with it.
moments.takeaway: Audit firm and client failed together.

moments.title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
moments.body: Sarbanes-Oxley introduces stricter financial reporting and corporate governance requirements for US public companies.
moments.takeaway: Regulation followed catastrophe.

now.title: Governance after Enron
now.body: SOX, IFRS adoption and audit committee strengthening trace to Enron-era scandals.
now.open_questions: Have post-Enron reforms reduced fraud risk or shifted it?

items.reflection: Enron's case is taught in accounting, ethics, governance and strategy courses.

moments.title: Kodak invents digital camera
moments.body: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson builds the first digital camera prototype. Management sees no path to commercialise without cannibalising film.
moments.takeaway: Incumbents can invent the technology that disrupts them.

moments.title: Digital sales overtake film
moments.body: Digital camera sales surpass film cameras globally as Kodak struggles to pivot.
moments.takeaway: The market shift Kodak feared duly occurred.

moments.title: Kodak bankruptcy
moments.body: Kodak files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
moments.takeaway: Incumbents fail despite advance warning.

now.title: Innovation dilemmas today
now.body: Kodak is a standard teaching case for the innovator's dilemma. Smartphone cameras have largely displaced standalone cameras since.
now.open_questions: Which incumbents are repeating the Kodak pattern in AI?

items.reflection: Kodak invented the technology that destroyed it, then could not commit to it.

moments.title: Netflix offered to Blockbuster
moments.body: Hastings reportedly offers to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster declines.
moments.takeaway: Incumbents can refuse acquisitions that would later save them.

moments.title: Netflix launches streaming
moments.body: Netflix launches streaming service alongside DVD by mail, beginning the transition.
moments.takeaway: Business model transitions take years to play out.

moments.title: Blockbuster bankruptcy
moments.body: Blockbuster files for bankruptcy in September 2010.
moments.takeaway: Incumbent dominance can collapse in a decade.

now.title: Streaming wars
now.body: Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video and others compete in streaming, while content costs have escalated.
now.open_questions: Is streaming a sustainable business model at current content investment levels?

items.reflection: Blockbuster's late-fee revenue model created the customer pain Netflix exploited.

moments.title: Theranos founded
moments.body: Theranos is founded by Holmes after dropping out of Stanford. It claims revolutionary blood-testing technology.
moments.takeaway: Founder mythology often outruns technical reality.

moments.title: Wall Street Journal investigation
moments.body: Carreyrou's articles expose Theranos's technology as ineffective and its testing as relying on conventional analysers.
moments.takeaway: Investigative journalism remains crucial to corporate accountability.

moments.title: Holmes conviction
moments.body: Holmes is convicted of fraud in January 2022 and sentenced to over 11 years.
moments.takeaway: Founder accountability extended to startup fraud.

now.title: Silicon Valley accountability
now.body: Theranos has reshaped venture due diligence in regulated industries and is a standard case in business ethics.
now.open_questions: Has the Theranos case changed VC behaviour outside health tech?

items.reflection: Theranos remains the iconic Silicon Valley fraud case of the 2010s.

moments.title: UberCab founded
moments.body: Uber is founded in San Francisco as UberCab, initially targeting black-car services.
moments.takeaway: Platforms grew from small premium niches.

moments.title: UberX expansion
moments.body: UberX expansion brings non-professional drivers into the platform, triggering regulatory battles globally.
moments.takeaway: Scale created regulatory conflict.

moments.title: Uber UK workers ruling
moments.body: The Supreme Court rules Uber drivers are workers entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay.
moments.takeaway: Platform classification fights reached the highest UK court.

now.title: Gig economy regulation
now.body: California's AB5/Prop 22, EU Platform Work Directive and UK Supreme Court rulings reshape platform employment.
now.open_questions: Will platform regulation push gig work toward traditional employment or new categories?

items.reflection: Uber pioneered the playbook of scaling fast and litigating later.

moments.title: AirBed and Breakfast founded
moments.who: Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia, Nathan Blecharczyk
moments.body: Airbnb is founded in San Francisco; the founders rent air mattresses during a sold-out design conference.
moments.takeaway: Even iconic platforms began as small side projects.

moments.title: Regulatory pushback
moments.who: Cities including Berlin, New York, Paris
moments.body: Multiple cities introduce restrictions on short-term rentals to protect housing markets.
moments.takeaway: Platforms triggered local regulatory responses globally.

moments.title: Airbnb IPO
moments.body: Despite a COVID-induced bookings collapse, Airbnb completes a $47bn IPO in December 2020.
moments.takeaway: Platform IPOs continued even through pandemic disruption.

now.title: Short-term rental governance
now.body: Most major cities now regulate Airbnb-style rentals through registration, caps and tax collection.
now.open_questions: Can platforms be regulated effectively at city level given global scale?

items.reflection: Airbnb redefined hospitality and triggered ongoing debates about housing affordability.

moments.title: Patagonia founded
moments.body: Patagonia is founded from Chouinard's climbing equipment business, integrating environmental values from the start.
moments.takeaway: Founder values can shape long-run corporate identity.

moments.title: B-Corp certification launched
moments.body: B Lab launches B-Corp certification for companies meeting social and environmental performance standards.
moments.takeaway: Third-party certification institutionalised stakeholder business.

moments.title: Patagonia ownership transferred
moments.body: Chouinard transfers Patagonia ownership to a trust and non-profit, dedicating all profits to environmental causes.
moments.takeaway: Ownership structure can match purpose.

now.title: Purpose-driven business
now.body: B-Corps now number in the thousands. Climate tech and impact investing extend purpose-driven business into new domains.
now.open_questions: Can purpose-driven structures scale to dominant industries?

items.reflection: Patagonia's transfer of ownership stands as one of the most striking corporate-purpose moves of the 2020s.

moments.title: Subprime crisis begins
moments.body: Subprime mortgage defaults rise; Bear Stearns hedge funds collapse in July.
moments.takeaway: Crisis built up slowly before the catastrophic events.

moments.title: Lehman files Chapter 11
moments.body: On 15 September Lehman files the largest bankruptcy in US history, triggering global financial paralysis.
moments.takeaway: A single firm's failure could freeze global credit.

moments.title: Dodd-Frank Act
moments.body: Dodd-Frank introduces new financial regulation including the Volcker rule and CFPB.
moments.takeaway: Regulation followed crisis with the usual delay.

now.title: Post-crisis financial system
now.body: Higher capital requirements, stress testing and macroprudential tools shape the post-2008 financial system.
now.open_questions: Are post-2008 reforms adequate for current shadow banking and crypto risk?

items.reflection: Lehman remains the canonical case study of too-big-to-fail and government response.
